answerChoices.rationale: The limb retains findings of salvageability but is immediately threatened; current intracranial bleeding changes the suitability of thrombolysis.

answerChoices.label: Catheter-directed alteplase thrombolysis
answerChoices.rationale: This is a real revascularization method, but current intracranial hemorrhage is a decisive bleeding concern for lytic treatment.

answerChoices.label: Primary major limb amputation
answerChoices.rationale: Weak but present movement and an audible venous signal do not match the prior completely anesthetic/paralyzed irreversible-limb construct.

decisionNodes.explanation: First decide whether the limb is beyond salvage: retained movement and an audible venous signal differ from the fully anesthetic, paralyzed pattern with absent venous flow. The represented limb is immediately threatened. Then incorporate the active intracranial hemorrhage before choosing a revascularization method; urgent operative thromboembolectomy is the best offered initial procedure for this constructed anatomy. Exact bleeding contraindication and operative ranking require direct source/vascular-clinician review. No routine heparin order, lytic dose or historical hemorrhage time cutoff is inferred.

priorIndependentReview.title: Reassurance after a negative test
fairness: The learner must select the symptomatic cohort, use the negative-test denominator, then translate the residual event frequency into the supplied fictional action rule. The routine-screening cohort and sensitivity calculation are credible near-misses.

Arithmetic: NPV is 112/(112+12), approximately 90.3%; residual leak frequency is approximately 9.7%, exceeding the constructed 5% criterion. The keyed CT action is uniquely supported under that protocol.

Importance: high for diagnostic-test interpretation and avoiding false reassurance; the exact CRP pathway is not clinical guidance. Realism: this works as a clearly labeled research-methods exercise, not as a real postoperative leak exclusion policy.
No material wording, length, or component-convergence cue found. The explicit hypothetical-rule label is necessary to avoid inventing clinical thresholds, not an answer leak.
suggestions: Retain the cohort distinction and full denominator data.
Keep the fictional protocol conspicuous in all renderings and feedback; do not imply a negative CRP screen justifies deferring assessment of a symptomatic patient outside this exercise.

concept.displayName: Applying a negative result in its tested population
concept.learningObjective: Select the appropriate tested population and negative-result denominator before applying an explicitly hypothetical next-investigation rule.
concept.novelty: Tests the negative-result conditional probability, distinct from sensitivity/specificity and the existing positive-result prevalence task.
concept.conceptVersionReason: The original decision calculated one NPV. This version makes population transport and conditional residual frequency change the protocol action; it retains the old denominator concept rather than reset its history.
concept.historyMigration: None. Preserved meanings retain IDs; materially changed constructs use new IDs and leave old histories intact.

clinicalCase.displayName: Reassurance after a negative test
clinicalCase.presentation: Helen Porter, a 64-year-old woman, attends clinic after colorectal surgery. During the admission, new fever and tachycardia led the team to order the study's investigational CRP-based leak screen; its result was negative. The study enrolled routine-screening and symptom-workup groups separately. Its hypothetical teaching protocol calls for contrast CT when the applicable cohort's residual leak frequency after a negative screen exceeds 5%; otherwise it calls for repeat CRP surveillance. This is an unvalidated constructed protocol, not a clinical rule for excluding a leak.

decisionNodes.stem: Which negative predictive value and protocol action apply to Helen Porter's negative screen?

answerChoices.label: 90.3% NPV; obtain contrast CT under the study protocol
answerChoices.rationale: For symptom workup, 112 of 124 negative screens are reference-negative: NPV 90.3%, residual frequency 9.7%, above the stated protocol trigger.

answerChoices.label: 98.7% NPV; repeat CRP surveillance under the study protocol
answerChoices.rationale: This imports the routine-screening group's 152/154 NPV and misses the higher residual frequency in the group corresponding to this order.

answerChoices.label: 80.0% NPV; obtain contrast CT under the study protocol
answerChoices.rationale: 48/60 is sensitivity in the symptom-workup group. It conditions on reference-positive cases rather than on this patient's negative result.

decisionNodes.explanation: First match the order's purpose to the study population, then condition on a negative result. The symptom-workup row has 112 true-negative and 12 false-negative screens: 112/(112+12) is 90.3%, leaving 9.7% reference-positive among negative screens. That exceeds this fictional protocol's 5% trigger, so its next step is contrast CT. The 98.7% result belongs to a different population, and 80% is sensitivity, not NPV. These constructed frequencies are not an individual's validated leak probability or a safe clinical discharge rule.
sourceLabels: Principles of Epidemiology: Lesson 5, Appendix A
Antibody (Serology) Testing for COVID-19: Information for Patients and Consumers

priorIndependentReview.title: Comparing positive-result frequency across reference groups
fairness: The unequal reference-group sizes require rates rather than positive counts, followed by likelihood-ratio updating of the provided odds and application of a stated study rule.

Arithmetic: sensitivity is 40/80=0.5, false-positive rate is 20/200=0.1, LR+ is 5, post-test odds are 1.25, and probability is 1.25/2.25, approximately 56%. This uniquely selects CT under the fictional protocol.

Importance: high for evidence interpretation; bedside calculation is less routine than the general lesson about pretest risk. Realism: appropriate as a constructed study discussion, with transferability explicitly assumed.
The 33% count-ratio error and 67% sample-PPV error are credible. No exploitable unique wording or component-convergence cue found.
suggestions: Retain the unequal denominators and supplied stratum odds; they make both inference steps consequential.
Keep the fictional threshold and transferability assumption explicit and do not present this as an empirically validated CRP care pathway.

concept.displayName: A positive screen and a prespecified investigation rule
concept.learningObjective: Use conditional test rates from unequal groups to update prior odds and apply a specified hypothetical investigation protocol.
concept.novelty: Tests a diagnostic evidence ratio between reference groups, rather than a predictive probability, treatment risk ratio or conditional odds ratio.
concept.conceptVersionReason: The original construct calculated LR+ without a patient consequence. This version adds prior-to-posterior updating that changes the next investigation; the original LR concept remains intact.
concept.historyMigration: None. Preserved meanings retain IDs; materially changed constructs use new IDs and leave old histories intact.

clinicalCase.displayName: Comparing positive-result frequency across reference groups
clinicalCase.presentation: George Allen, a 58-year-old man, reviews his participation in a constructed postoperative-complication study. At the point in question, the investigational CRP screen was positive. The study assigned pretest odds of the target complication of 1:4 for his enrollment stratum. Its teaching protocol obtains contrast CT when the post-test probability is at least 50% and repeats the screen below that value. The investigators assume the displayed test characteristics transfer to his stratum. These odds and action rules are fictional inputs, not clinical thresholds.

decisionNodes.stem: Which post-test probability and protocol action follow from George Allen's positive screen?

answerChoices.label: 56%; CT acquisition
answerChoices.rationale: Sensitivity is 40/80 and false-positive rate 20/200, so LR+ is 5. Prior odds 1/4 become 5/4; probability is 5/9, approximately 56%.

answerChoices.label: 33%; repeat CRP assay
answerChoices.rationale: Using the raw positive counts 40/20 as the likelihood ratio gives 2 and then post-test odds 1/2, but the unequal reference-group sizes require rates.

answerChoices.label: 67%; CT acquisition
answerChoices.rationale: 40/60 is the positive predictive value within the validation sample. Its selected reference-group mix differs from the patient's stated prior odds.

decisionNodes.explanation: Calculate conditional rates before updating this patient's prior odds. Sensitivity is 0.5 and the false-positive rate is 0.1, giving LR+ 5. Multiplying pretest odds 1:4 by 5 gives 5:4; 5/(5+4) is approximately 56%. That reaches this fictional protocol's CT branch. Dividing raw positive counts happens to work only under special sample-size relationships and fails here. The validation sample's 40/60 positive fraction also uses a different prior mix. The result depends on the stated transport assumption and supplies no real test validation or patient-risk estimate.
sourceLabels: Principles of Epidemiology: Lesson 5, Appendix A
Public Health Technical Guidance: Odds ratio and relative risk

priorIndependentReview.title: Absolute adverse-event increase and number needed to harm

cues.phrase: NNT 34 / NNH 20; revise
cues.why: Component convergence favors the key without arithmetic: NNT 34 appears twice and 'revise' appears twice, and only the key combines those majority components.

fairness: Arithmetic is correct: absolute infection reduction is 0.03, giving NNT 34 under the stated round-up rule; absolute rash increase is 0.05, giving NNH 20. The benefit criterion is met and the harm criterion is not, so the specified next-phase result is revise.

Importance: high for distinguishing absolute benefit and harm. Realism: acceptable as an explicitly fictional research progression rule; it is not sufficient real-world evidence for adopting or rejecting treatment without uncertainty and clinical weighting.

Calculating both absolute effects and applying the joint decision rule provides genuine two-step quantitative work, but the option construction undermines it. No competing key or clinical threshold error is asserted.
suggestions: Rebuild the options so repeated NNT and decision components do not uniquely assemble the key; use a balanced set of credible calculation errors with decisions consistently derived from each stated result.
Retain separate benefit and harm event counts and the explicit fictional prespecified criteria. Recheck convergence after rewriting, not just numerical correctness.

qualityReview.coverKeyAttack: Three distinct numerical pairs derive from absolute effects, comparator risks or regimen risks. No numerical component repeats across pairs; the twice-occurring revision action cannot assemble a result. Labels retain the same grammar and detail.
qualityReview.sameStageAndCategory: Three calculated benefit/harm results with the decision consistently derived from each stated pair.
qualityReview.interpretFindings: Calculate absolute between-group effects rather than invert a single-arm rate, keeping both outcomes over the same horizon.
qualityReview.applyFindings: Apply the prespecified benefit and harm requirements jointly rather than advance on infection benefit alone.
qualityReview.difficultyReason: The plausible wrong computations retain the right direction and often the same phase decision; both exact absolute quantities must still be calculated.
qualityReview.singleBestAnswer: Only NNT 34 and NNH 20 follow from the actual differences; the stated joint rule then requires revision.
qualityReview.closestError: Invert the comparator's rash risk instead of the added risk caused by the new regimen.
qualityReview.counterfactual: An actual excess of 3% with the same infection benefit would produce NNH 34 and meet the stated progression criterion.

reviewerResponse.cues: Replaced repeated NNT components with three distinct complete numerical pairs; rechecked that no repeated quantity assembles the key.
reviewerResponse.fairness: Kept the correct arithmetic, common horizon, explicit fictional criteria and limited next-study consequence.
reviewerResponse.suggestions: Each wrong result derives from a specified rate-versus-difference error and its decision is consistent with that result. No new clinical threshold is asserted.

priorIndependentReview.title: A paired binary change needs a paired analysis
fairness: The linked records call for paired binary analysis, and net improvement is (12-5)/100=7 percentage points, below the supplied 10-point rule. McNemar with revision is the best offered combination. Merely using Fisher on marginal totals would lose the pairing.
The paired-data description is necessary design information, not an unfair cue. The balanced four-option matrix has no component-frequency advantage.

Importance: moderate to high for interpreting paired quality audits. Realism is the weakness: 'A recorded answer' is unspecified, so it is unclear whether the checklist changes actual medication reconciliation, corrects an audit response, or retests reviewers on the same records. suggestions: Define the binary endpoint concretely, such as completion of a specified medication-reconciliation action against a documented reference, and identify who performed each before/after assessment.

clinicalCase.displayName: A paired binary change needs a paired analysis
clinicalCase.presentation: Terry Wilson, a 62-year-old man, reviews a clinic medication-reconciliation pilot in which his record participated. A pharmacist established a reference medication list for each of 100 patients using interview and medicine-container review. For each reference record, the same clerk first entered a preoperative medication list by the old workflow, then re-entered it using the proposed checklist; an independent pharmacist compared both versions with the same reference. The binary endpoint was omission of at least one current prescribed medicine versus no such omission. Record identifiers were retained. A fictional feasibility plan advances to a controlled study only if the proportion without an omission improves by at least 10 percentage points; otherwise the checklist is revised. This is not a causal trial or permission for clinical rollout.

decisionNodes.explanation: The two medication-list outputs refer to the same patient reference record, so they are not independent samples. McNemar's paired-binary analysis uses the discordant outcomes. The no-omission proportion rises from 48/100 to 55/100: a seven-point net improvement after accounting for five records that worsened. The fictional plan therefore calls for checklist revision before a controlled phase. Repeating the task in the same order may introduce learning and order effects; this uncontrolled audit does not establish causal benefit, regardless of the selected paired analysis.

priorIndependentReview.title: Equivalence requires the prespecified margin comparison
fairness: The learner must separate recovery equivalence from adequate precision of the serious-complication estimate. The nonsignificant null p-value is a credible distraction rather than proof of safety equivalence.

The recovery 90% interval lies within the stated equivalence bounds, while the complication upper 95% limit of 3.2 exceeds the protocol's 2-point ceiling. Withholding replacement and obtaining better complication precision is the best offered plan under the supplied rule.

Importance: high for interpreting trials and pathway implementation. Realism: a committee protocol discussion is plausible, although more precise complication evidence is a research need rather than a guaranteed feasible or successful next study.
The hypothetical margins are appropriately disclosed. No material cue or numeric inconsistency found; the p-value is approximately compatible with the displayed normal-approximation interval.
suggestions: Retain both outcomes and the null-test distraction; neither outcome alone should settle the decision.
Keep feedback clear that failure of the adoption criterion is insufficient evidence of acceptable safety, not proof that the new pathway causes excess harm.

concept.displayName: Recovery equivalence with an unresolved safety requirement
concept.learningObjective: Distinguish a met equivalence endpoint from an unresolved safety bound when choosing the next study and implementation stage.
concept.novelty: Tests a positive equivalence decision from a prespecified margin and the corresponding interval, rather than null-effect significance, precision or power.
concept.conceptVersionReason: The original construct interpreted one equivalence interval. This version uses two separate endpoint requirements to select a consequential implementation/research plan.
concept.historyMigration: None. Preserved meanings retain IDs; materially changed constructs use new IDs and leave old histories intact.

clinicalCase.displayName: Equivalence requires the prespecified margin comparison
clinicalCase.presentation: Agnes Hill, a 63-year-old woman, attends clinic after a constructed randomized comparison of postoperative pathways. The committee's prespecified teaching protocol adopts the new pathway only if recovery meets its TOST equivalence requirement and the upper 95% confidence limit for added serious complications is below 2 percentage points. The protocol and results are shown below. Its margins are hypothetical study inputs, not universal clinical tolerances.

decisionNodes.explanation: Interpret each endpoint against its own prespecified criterion. The recovery 90% interval is entirely within -2 to +2 days, meeting the stated TOST equivalence condition. The complication interval still extends beyond +2 percentage points, so that separate requirement is unresolved. A null-difference p-value of 0.78 does not establish a sufficiently small added harm. Under this constructed protocol, retain the current pathway and focus further study on the safety endpoint. This is not proof that the new pathway is harmful, nor a real adoption threshold.

priorIndependentReview.title: Comparing outcomes at a common surgical case mix
fairness: Within each pathway, straightforward risk is 10% and complex risk is 40%; applying the specified equal weights gives 25% for both. The 13%/37% option uses the observed unequal case mix, and 10%/40% confuses stratum risks with pathway risks.
The answer is unique and the options are parallel. Equal weights do not reveal the equal answer without calculating or recognizing the shared stratum-specific risks.
Importance: high for interpreting surgical outcome comparisons. Realism: this is an appropriate constructed report discussion, with a specified standard population and no unsupported causal claim.

This is a focused applied standardization calculation, not an interpretation followed by a separate management decision; twoStep is therefore false. It can still be moderately challenging because the denominator/case-mix error is substantive. The exact frozen v1 remains unchanged.
suggestions: Retain the equal-weight comparison and both denominator structures. Do not imply standardization alone proves the pathways causally equivalent.
If a later version is meant to test a second decision, add a meaningful reporting or comparison choice that actually depends on the standardized result; preserve this frozen version.

concept.displayName: Comparing outcomes at a common surgical case mix
concept.learningObjective: Calculate directly standardized outcome risks using a common specified stratum distribution rather than compare crude rates from different case mixes.
concept.novelty: Tests a quantitative common-case-mix comparison, rather than merely naming confounding or dividing crude risks.

clinicalCase.displayName: Comparing outcomes at a common surgical case mix
clinicalCase.presentation: Felix Martin, a 66-year-old man, discusses a constructed report comparing two surgical pathways. The groups contain different proportions of straightforward and complex procedures. To compare the observed stratum-specific risks at the same case mix, the report specifies equal 50% weights for the two procedure strata.

approvedInstantiationProfiles.presentation: Felix Martin, a 66-year-old man, discusses a constructed report comparing two surgical pathways. The groups contain different proportions of straightforward and complex procedures. To compare the observed stratum-specific risks at the same case mix, the report specifies equal 50% weights for the two procedure strata.

sourceLabels: Analyzing and Interpreting Data

decisionNodes.stem: What standardized event risks result from the specified equal case mix in the report discussed with Felix Martin?

answerChoices.label: A: 25%; B: 25%
answerChoices.rationale: Each pathway has stratum risks 10% and 40%; weighting each by 0.5 gives 25% for both.

answerChoices.label: A: 13%; B: 37%
answerChoices.rationale: These are the crude risks, which preserve the different procedure mixes rather than apply the specified common weights.

answerChoices.label: A: 10%; B: 40%
answerChoices.rationale: This selects a different stratum for each pathway rather than standardizing both to the same distribution.

decisionNodes.explanation: At the given common weights, each risk is 0.5×0.10 + 0.5×0.40 = 0.25. Different crude rates reflect the different represented case mixes. This constructed arithmetic does not prove a causal effect or exclude other biases in a real observational comparison.

statementMapping.constructedDataBasis: Finite fictional observations/datasets for application; not empirical probabilities, demographic disease weights, guideline thresholds or actual service durations.

claims.statement: Surgical antimicrobial prophylaxis should be discontinued after incision closure; continuing it solely because a drain remains does not reduce surgical-site infection and adds antimicrobial harms.
claims.limitation: This concerns prophylaxis only, not treatment for an established infection or another therapeutic indication. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review. Only one recorded source publication supports this atomic claim; no independent management cross-check has been added.
claims.applicablePopulation: Postoperative adults with a closed incision, no established infection, and a prophylactic antibiotic continued solely because a drain remains.

claims.statement: For a patient receiving warfarin for atrial fibrillation who requires interruption for elective surgery, routine therapeutic-dose heparin bridging is not recommended.
claims.limitation: Selected very-high-thromboembolic-risk situations require individualized consideration; this does not concern ordinary postoperative VTE prophylaxis or mechanical-valve cases. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review. Only one recorded source publication supports this atomic claim; no independent management cross-check has been added.
claims.applicablePopulation: Selected adults taking warfarin for nonvalvular atrial fibrillation without recent stroke, TIA, thrombosis, a mechanical valve, or another very-high-risk feature.

claims.statement: After major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery, selected patients with high VTE risk and acceptable bleeding risk may receive extended postoperative pharmacologic prophylaxis for up to about four weeks; LMWH is an established option.
claims.limitation: This is not universal for all cancer operations, and LMWH is not the only current agent; patient selection, renal function, and bleeding risk matter. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Selected high-VTE-risk adults after major abdominal or pelvic cancer surgery with adequate renal function and low bleeding risk.

claims.statement: A localized superficial incisional surgical-site infection with purulence requires opening the involved incision and drainage, with removal of sutures or staples when needed for source control.
claims.limitation: Systemic antibiotics depend on systemic response and operative site; deep, organ-space, and necrotizing infections require different care. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review. Only one recorded source publication supports this atomic claim; no independent management cross-check has been added.
claims.applicablePopulation: Stable adults with purulent superficial incisional infection, intact fascia, and no systemic toxicity.

claims.statement: A patient with uncomplicated peptic ulcer disease who has not been evaluated for Helicobacter pylori should receive an active-infection test such as a urea breath test or stool antigen test rather than antibody serology.
claims.limitation: PPIs, antibiotics, and bismuth can reduce test sensitivity. The authored patients have completed appropriate medication holds and have no bleeding or acute complication. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Stable adults with a known uncomplicated duodenal ulcer who need initial H. pylori evaluation.

claims.statement: After H. pylori treatment, eradication should be confirmed with an active-infection test at least four weeks after antibiotics, with PPIs held for two weeks and antibiotics or bismuth held for four weeks.
claims.limitation: This is a future follow-up plan. The game visit does not simulate treatment completion or the washout interval, and serology is not a test of cure. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review. Only one recorded source publication supports this atomic claim; no independent management cross-check has been added.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with confirmed H. pylori infection for whom treatment and subsequent eradication confirmation are being planned.

claims.statement: After failed appropriate medical treatment, lateral internal sphincterotomy can be discussed for selected chronic anal fissure when baseline fecal incontinence and stated continence-risk history are absent.
claims.limitation: LIS requires individualized continence counseling and is not suitable for every patient. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Stable adults with chronic fissure persistent after documented medical treatment and no described continence risk.

claims.statement: For a typical chronic anal fissure, topical calcium-channel-blocker treatment is an appropriate first-line pharmacologic option with comparable efficacy and fewer adverse effects than topical nitrates.
claims.limitation: No drug, concentration, schedule, duration, or individual contraindication is taught. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Stable adults with clinician-characterized chronic midline anal fissure.

claims.statement: Localized resectable colon cancer is treated by resection of the tumor-bearing colon together with its regional lymphatic drainage.
claims.limitation: Operation extent depends on anatomy and patient factors; this claim does not select disputed splenic-flexure techniques or adjuvant therapy without pathological stage. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with localized resectable colon adenocarcinoma and no distant or adjacent-organ invasion on staging.

claims.statement: After CT assesses postoperative collections, contrast-enhanced MRCP with a hepatobiliary agent can anatomically localize a suspected bile leak and evaluate duct continuity; scintigraphy can demonstrate active leakage but has limited spatial detail.
claims.limitation: The dedicated hepatobiliary-contrast study is a distinct external service; this claim does not make MRCP the first test in an unstable patient. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review. Only one recorded source publication supports this atomic claim; no independent management cross-check has been added.
claims.applicablePopulation: Stable post-cholecystectomy adults after CT excludes an uncontrolled collection.

claims.statement: A persistent minor postoperative bile leak with preserved common-duct continuity can be referred for ERCP with transpapillary plastic-stent treatment.
claims.limitation: Excludes sepsis, peritonitis, uncontrolled collections, and complete common-bile-duct or common-hepatic-duct transection. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Stable patients with a persistent minor post-cholecystectomy leak and preserved duct continuity.

claims.statement: A common-bile-duct stone confirmed on MRCP requires a therapeutic duct-clearance pathway; preoperative therapeutic ERCP is one accepted pathway when that sequence is selected locally.
claims.limitation: Postoperative ERCP and laparoscopic duct treatment are also valid according to local expertise; the cases explicitly select the preoperative endoscopic pathway. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Stable treatment candidates with a confirmed duct stone before planned cholecystectomy.

claims.statement: Contrast-enhanced CT can characterize a post-pancreatitis fluid collection before drainage planning; a mature encapsulated homogeneous fluid collection without solid debris after interstitial edematous pancreatitis is compatible with a pancreatic pseudocyst rather than walled-off necrosis.
claims.limitation: The case must exclude necrotizing pancreatitis, pseudoaneurysm, and suspicious neoplastic features; no diameter alone establishes a drainage indication. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Stable adults with persistent symptoms after resolved interstitial edematous acute pancreatitis.

claims.statement: A symptomatic mature pancreatic pseudocyst with suitable apposition to the stomach or duodenum can be referred for EUS-guided endoscopic drainage when appropriate expertise and backup are available.
claims.limitation: Symptoms, maturity, and suitable anatomy are required; this is an external specialist referral and size alone is not an indication. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Stable patients with a characterized symptomatic pseudocyst and suitable anatomy.

claims.statement: Neoadjuvant imatinib is a multidisciplinary option when an imatinib-sensitive, locally advanced GIST would benefit from shrinkage that reduces operative morbidity; size or high-risk features alone are insufficient.
claims.limitation: No dose, duration, response interval, postoperative therapy, or universal size rule is taught. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Adults with tissue-confirmed, nonmetastatic, imatinib-sensitive GIST and a challenging but potentially improved resection after response.

claims.statement: EUS-guided core tissue acquisition with molecular analysis is appropriate when a gastric subepithelial lesion is locally advanced and preoperative targeted treatment is being considered; routine biopsy is not required before every straightforward resection.
claims.limitation: Core sampling is selected because immediate planning needs histology and genotype; a limited core does not establish definitive mitotic-risk classification. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Stable adults with a nonmetastatic gastric subepithelial mass whose location would make immediate resection substantially morbid.

claims.statement: A GCS total is the sum of eye, verbal, and motor scores only when all three components are testable; components should remain visible.
claims.limitation: No severity band, prognosis, or treatment threshold is taught. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review.
claims.applicablePopulation: Patients with all three GCS components testable.

claims.statement: Eye response scores are E4 spontaneous, E3 to sound, E2 to pressure, and E1 none.
claims.limitation: Official source family; independent corroboration limited. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review. Only one recorded source publication supports this atomic claim; no independent management cross-check has been added.
claims.applicablePopulation: Patients undergoing GCS assessment.

claims.statement: Motor response scores are M6 obeys commands, M5 localizes, M4 normal flexion, M3 abnormal flexion, M2 extension, and M1 none.
claims.limitation: Official source family; independent corroboration limited. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review. Only one recorded source publication supports this atomic claim; no independent management cross-check has been added.
claims.applicablePopulation: Patients undergoing GCS assessment.

claims.statement: When an interference genuinely prevents verbal testing, document V-NT with the reason and do not substitute 1 or 0 or report a misleading total.
claims.limitation: A tracheostomy does not automatically make speech untestable. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2. The exact clinical application, decision boundary and option ranking require review.

claims.limitation: Single current society guideline; energy needs and tolerance remain individualized. Offline reuse: source verification and currentness have not been refreshed for N2.
